author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts health officials have confirmed the state’s 12th human case of West Nile virus this year, and Milton and Quincy have been moved into the high-risk category. The Massachusetts Department of Public Health said in its Oct. 2 [announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/state-health-officials-announce-12th-human-case-of-west-nile-virus-in-massachusetts) that the patient is a woman in her 60s who was likely exposed in Norfolk County. [Boston.com independently reported the case and the two community-level risk changes](https://www.boston.com/news/local-news/2026/10/02/mass-health-officials-announce-12th-human-case-of-west-nile-virus/).

The new designations make Milton and Quincy the latest communities where DPH is urging heightened attention to mosquito exposure. The department continues to list Boston, Brookline, Cambridge, Chelsea, Everett, Malden, Newton, Revere, Somerville, Watertown and Winthrop at high risk. Most of the rest of Massachusetts is at moderate risk, according to DPH, and the seasonal threat will continue until the state experiences its first hard frost.

The statewide case count is part of a broader surveillance picture. DPH said Massachusetts detected its first West Nile-positive mosquitoes of the season on June 16, and 340 mosquito samples had tested positive by Oct. 2 across 13 counties: Barnstable, Berkshire, Bristol, Dukes, Essex, Franklin, Hampden, Hampshire, Middlesex, Norfolk, Plymouth, Suffolk and Worcester. Positive mosquito samples indicate where the virus has been detected in mosquitoes; they are not additional human cases.

The department reported no animal cases of West Nile virus this year. It is also tracking Eastern equine encephalitis, or EEE, a separate mosquito-borne virus. Twenty-seven mosquito samples had tested positive for EEE, while Massachusetts had reported no human or animal EEE cases as of the Oct. 2 update. Keeping those figures separate matters because the two viruses have different surveillance counts even though the same mosquito-control precautions can reduce exposure to both.

The latest case is an update to the 11-case total DPH announced on Sept. 25, when the department described three additional cases involving people exposed or likely exposed in Suffolk and Middlesex counties. The new Norfolk County case shows why the state’s risk map can change as human cases and mosquito testing add information. A high designation is a public-health warning for the community, not a claim that every outdoor location or every mosquito carries the virus.

DPH recommends using an EPA-registered insect repellent according to its label, wearing long sleeves, long pants and socks outdoors, and considering the timing of outdoor activities because many mosquitoes are most active from dusk to dawn. Residents can also reduce breeding sites by emptying containers that collect water, checking gutters and drains, changing birdbath water frequently and keeping window and door screens tight.

For Milton, Quincy and the other high-risk communities, the practical message is to keep those steps in place even as cooler weather arrives. The state says risk remains until the first hard frost, so a late-season evening outdoors can still bring exposure. Animal owners should remove standing water and consult veterinarians about repellents and vaccinations approved for horses and other animals, DPH said.

The department updates case information, positive mosquito results and local risk levels through its [Massachusetts Arbovirus Update](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massachusetts-arbovirus-update) page. Those daily updates are the best way for residents to track whether their community’s designation changes. For now, the confirmed development is both a new human case and a wider high-risk map, while state surveillance continues through the end of mosquito season.
dek: A woman in her 60s was likely exposed in Norfolk County; state officials now list Milton and Quincy at high risk alongside 11 other communities.
headline: Massachusetts confirms 12th West Nile case as Milton, Quincy risk rises
seoDescription: Massachusetts confirms a 12th human West Nile case and raises risk levels in Milton and Quincy as mosquito surveillance continues.
seoTitle: 12th West Nile case raises risk in Milton and Quincy
